title: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
author: Matt Grant
content:
Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went
before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch
to bring in more money for policing.

His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the
business of immigration enforcement.

“I won’t say there's unlimited funding, but there's quite a bit of money in
the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in
which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs
Enforcement.

He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego
received $100,000.

It stands to earn much more.

Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could
bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east
of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already
received, that's roughly equivalent to 40% of the town's $2.1 million police
budget last year.

Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-
September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President
Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in
these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers
to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key
incentive for local governments across the country has [long been the funding
that comes with participation](https://www.wsj.com/us-news/immigration-
arrests-police-trump-f0ca5253?st=uHJuav&reflink=article_copyURL_share).

The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while
requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is
spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found
that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to
their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments.

The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police
chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar
pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time
spent,” he said.

And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county
commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature”
could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and
money for overtime.

“How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner
John Moore asked.

“Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.

Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local
law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it
difficult to pull away from the program in the future.

“I'm concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of
these small police departments,” she said.

In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all
the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations,
in addition to immigration work.  

The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January
to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to
records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By
this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay
for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and
“fleet purchases.”

Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our
everyday job,” Fowler said.

Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help
officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not
respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a
statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets
dangerous criminal offenders.

Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN's questions about the
department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated
attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by
phone, email and in person.

"We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie
Galloway, the only official to respond.

Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a
conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can
help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for
overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money
is spent.

KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s
Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300
people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60
days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if
an agreement is terminated.

That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get
federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and
keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council
members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.

Between the end of April and mid-June, it made two.

![A tan concrete building with tall windows, metal awnings over glass double
doors bearing sheriff seals, and green shrubbery along a brick-paved street in
bright daylight.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261114-Tavitian-287gTexasMoney-41_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)The
Smith County Sheriff’s Office, based in Tyler, Texas, received nearly $2.2
million in funding through 287(g) from January 2025 through June 2026, more
than any other department reviewed by KXAN. Antranik Tavitian for ProPublica
and The Texas Tribune

### “Are You a U.S. Citizen?”

Local law enforcement agencies that join forces with ICE can choose among
three models, two of which focus on identifying people already in jail who may
be subject to deportation.

Trump revived the third kind, called the task force model, at the beginning of
his second term. Task force agreements often worry civil and immigrants’
rights groups because of the model’s problematic track record: ICE started
phasing them out in 2012, after Department of Justice investigations revealed
that sheriff’s offices participating in the model had committed civil rights
violations.

But task force agreements can also be lucrative.

Agencies can receive federal reimbursement for salaries, overtime and benefits
for “conducting purposeful and intentional” immigration enforcement activities
once the contract starts, according to a service agreement obtained by KXAN.

They can also get recurring quarterly incentive payments and one-time stipends
for equipment, technology and vehicles, though federal memoranda and
agreements obtained by KXAN don't specify what agencies can purchase.

The Department of Homeland Security stopped renewing task force model
agreements [during the Obama administration
after](https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/fy-2012-ice-announces-year-end-
removal-numbers-highlights-focus-key-priorities-and) federal investigations
revealed civil rights violations involving [sheriffs’ offices in
Arizona](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/department-justice-releases-
investigative-findings-maricopa-county-sheriff-s-office) and[ North
Carolina](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/justice-department-releases-
investigative-findings-alamance-county-nc-sheriff-s-office).

Since Trump’s return to office, the model has become the most common of the
three agreement types. At least 241 task force model agreements were signed in
Texas in 2026 alone, compared to just 30 combined for the other models in that
time period, according to ICE participation data from September.

Smith County was among the first in Texas to sign on after the president
reinstated the task force model in early 2025.  

Moore, the only member of [Smith County](https://www.smith-
county.com/280/Precinct-2)’s Commissioners Court who agreed to speak with
KXAN, explained why he thought the commissioners wanted to partner.

His first word: “budgetary.”

“Any kind of training that any of our departments need to have, or are
required to have, costs money, and it's rare that we get an opportunity to get
funding for training from outside county taxes,” Moore said. “Any time we can
save the taxpayers money, I'm all for it.”

Smith County got more money than any other of the 93 Texas law enforcement
agencies whose funding KXAN reviewed. The sheriff’s office received nearly
$2.2 million in federal 287(g) funding from January 2025 to June 2026,
according to records obtained by KXAN. That’s equivalent to about 12% of its
budget for fiscal year 2025.

Smith, the sheriff, told the Commissioners Court last November that although
vehicles purchased with that money would be used for the 287(g) program, “that
doesn’t mean, if we’re out here, we won’t run to another call or take another
call that comes across the radio. We will do that. We try not to separate
287(g) from our other law enforcement duties. We do it all together.”

About 120 of 198 licensed officers in the Smith County Sheriff’s Office
participated in the program. Together, they conducted 124 immigration
enforcement actions between October 2025 and July. KXAN requested a list of
287(g) stops from the department, in addition to any associated charge. Smith
County listed no associated criminal charge for more than 100 of these stops.

![A row of white Smith County Sheriff patrol SUVs is parked side by side
inside a garage.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261114-Tavitian-287gTexasMoney-33_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)The
Smith County Sheriff’s Office took 124 immigration enforcement actions between
October 2025 and July, though no criminal charge was associated with over 100
of those actions. Antranik Tavitian for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune

Jose Rodriguez and his 23-year-old son, Pablo Rodriguez, were among those
affected.

One afternoon in late June, the pair cruised along Loop 323, a circular
segment of highway in Tyler, a city of 113,000 people in East Texas. They’d
spent hours working in the summer heat at a construction job and were headed
to Chick-fil-A to pick up lunch for their family.

Then red and blue lights appeared behind them. The law enforcement agent said
that he’d pulled their black extended-cab work truck over because of a missing
license plate on the trailer attached to the pickup and a missing dual-wheel
mud flap.

Body and vehicle camera footage showed the detective requesting that Jose
Rodriguez get out of the truck. “Any English at all?” the detective later
asked. Jose Rodriguez raised his right hand, holding his thumb and index
finger close together.

“Un poquito?” the detective asked, followed by, “Are you a U.S. citizen?”

The man shook his head and answered. “No.”

Seconds later, the detective pulled Jose Rodriguez’s hands behind his back and
put him in handcuffs.

He was eventually taken from the Smith County jail to an ICE detention
facility, about two hours west of Tyler. His son, who is a U.S. citizen, said
Jose Rodriguez was detained for about three months before being deported to
Mexico.

KXAN could find no criminal convictions or arrests on his record when the
Smith County detective took him into custody in June.

“Just like that, he’s gone,” Pablo Rodriguez later told KXAN. “My dad’s gone.”

Law enforcement officers, Pablo Rodriguez said, “portray us as criminals,
rapists, violent people. We’re not that. We’re just regular people trying to
find a better life. The only difference is our skin. That’s pretty much it.”

![A young man wearing a light gray knit beanie, an olive green Nike hoodie,
light-wash jeans and work boots stands outdoors in front of a wire fence and
sunlit trees.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261114-Tavitian-287gTexasMoney-11_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)

T-shirt and blue jeans crouching outdoors while holding a leafy
stem.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/20261114-Tavitian-287gTexasMoney-15_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)

Pablo Rodriguez, first image, shows a photo of his father, Jose Rodriguez, on
his phone. Jose Rodriguez was deported after the pair were stopped by a Smith
County Sheriff’s officer authorized to perform immigration duties under a
287(g) agreement. Antranik Tavitian for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune

### The Future of the Program in Texas

Elections earlier this month have left the 287(g) program's future uncertain,
at least in Texas.

While the Trump administration has reached agreements with local law
enforcement to work with immigration officials, Congress has broader oversight
authority. That includes decisions about funding. In January, Democrats will
take over both chambers of Congress and many, including freshman Texas Sen.
James Talarico, have criticized ICE tactics. It's unclear, however, how much
of their focus will be on immigration enforcement and specifically on the
287(g) program.  

More locally, state Sen. Charles Schwertner, the Republican lawmaker who
authored a measure in 2025 that required most Texas sheriff’s offices to
participate in the program, wants to expand the mandate during the coming
legislative session to include other law enforcement agencies, like police
departments. So does the conservative think tank where Blair works.

But support for such legislation may be harder to get after November’s midterm
election.

Schwertner retained his state Senate seat, and Republicans maintained their
majority in that chamber, but Democrats took control of the governor’s mansion
and the state House of Representatives for the first time in a generation. Any
new bills would require legislative approval from both chambers and the
governor’s signature, or enough legislative support to override a veto.

[In a press release well before the
election,](https://ginafortexas.com/2026/01/hinojosa-calls-on-abbott-to-stop-
facilitating-fatal-ice-operations/?utm_source=) Democrat Gina Hinojosa called
on Gov. Greg Abbott to “demand accountability from the Trump administration
and stop enabling ICE operations that are terrorizing communities and
violating the law.” The release did not mention the 287(g) program by name.
Hinojosa beat Abbott in this month’s election and will take over as governor
in January. She did not respond to a request for comment for this story.

The state program could also be affected by this month’s election of Democrats
[Nathan Johnson](https://nathanfortexas.com/), who won the race for state
attorney general, and [Sarah Eckhardt](https://www.saraheckhardt.com/), who
won her bid to become state comptroller.

Johnson, as a state senator, opposed the mandate that sheriffs' offices
participate in the program. He will inherit responsibility for enforcing the
law, which requires most sheriffs to seek agreements with ICE by Dec. 1.
Johnson said he will use his discretion in deciding whether to sue sheriffs
who fail to comply if they have “legitimate law enforcement reasons for not
having a 287(g) agreement.”

He also questioned the state attorney general’s continued participation in the
program. Current Attorney General Ken Paxton [signed a 287(g) task force model
agreement in February
2025.](https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/news/releases/attorney-general-
ken-paxton-becomes-first-texas-law-enforcement-official-sign-agreement-help-0)

“The attorney general’s office has tremendous, vast responsibilities,” Johnson
said. “Never included among them since the creation of this state was
outsourcing your employees to a federal agency for a purpose in which we’re
not trained or qualified and which distracts me from the mission of my
office.”

Johnson didn’t entirely rule out working with ICE in some capacity if it
allowed his office to investigate crimes committed by ICE agents in Texas.

Eckhardt, meanwhile, will take over oversight of a $20 million grant program
that state lawmakers created two years ago to help sheriff’s offices cover any
costs of participation in the 287(g) program not reimbursed by the federal
government. By late September, the comptroller’s office had awarded more than
$6.5 million to 78 sheriff’s offices, according to figures obtained by KXAN.

During her campaign, Eckhardt warned that expenses for the program could
eventually fall on local taxpayers, calling it “unsustainable.” After winning
her seat, she said she would “do a 287(g) audit to show how that expense is
driving up property taxes.”

### Read More

This story is an adaptation of an investigation by KXAN. Read the original
reporting:

[Shadow Force: Texas' ICE-Powered Police Network](https://www.kxan.com/shadow-

Even if state leaders don’t expand the participation requirement or remove the
current mandate, departments can choose to keep collecting federal money to
enforce immigration law.

In Fayette County southeast of Austin, Sheriff’s Lt. David Beyer told KXAN
that the 287(g) funding his office had already received totaled about
$800,000, which helps purchase equipment it can also use for ordinary police
work.

“If they want to pay us extra to do that job,” Beyer said, “we're more than
happily going to accept those funds, because that saves our taxpayers money.”
